summary: Describes using the TESLA transform from RFC 4082 within the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol. It provides data origin authentication for multicast and broadcast streams. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: When one person talks to a crowd, listeners want proof the voice is real. TESLA gives it by revealing a secret code a little later.

questions: how does tesla authenticate multicast streams
what are the default tesla srtp parameters
why does tesla delay key disclosure
subtitle: How to prove who sent each packet of a multicast media stream, using delayed key disclosure inside SRTP.

tldr.problem: In a group, everyone shares one key, so a normal MAC cannot show which member sent a packet. Digital signatures can, but they cost too much time and bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: TESLA adds three fields to each SRTP packet: an interval number, a key disclosed from an earlier interval, and a MAC made with a key that is revealed a few intervals later. Receivers buffer each packet until its key arrives, then verify it.
tldr.outcome: SRTP gains an optional transform that gives data origin authentication to group streams, at the price of delayed verification and about 38 extra bytes per packet with the defaults.

today: RFC 4383 is a Proposed Standard from February 2006. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on RFC 3711 and RFC 4082.

sections.title: Why Group Streams Need More Than a MAC
sections.content:
Multicast and broadcast applications often need data origin authentication: proof that a message came from a given source and was not changed on the way. Between two parties, a MAC under a key known only to them does this.

In a group, the key is shared by more than two members. Any member can then alter a packet or impersonate another member. The MAC only shows that the sender is somewhere inside the group. Digital signatures solve this, but they cost time to sign and verify and bandwidth to carry the signature.

This memo specifies TESLA (Timed Efficient Stream Loss-tolerant Authentication, defined in RFC 4082) for SRTP. It works so long as receivers abide by the TESLA security invariants.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone in a club shares one password, anyone can pretend to be anyone else. TESLA gives each speaker a way to prove it is really them.

sections.title: SRTP and TESLA Background
sections.content:
SRTP (RFC 3711) is a profile of RTP that provides confidentiality, message authentication and replay protection for RTP and RTCP traffic. It is a framework that lets new transforms be added, but it defines nothing for data origin authentication in group security associations. TESLA is added as an alternative message authentication algorithm.

TESLA gives delayed per-packet authentication. It also needs a synchronization protocol, so sender and receiver can compare clocks and bound the difference, and a bootstrapping procedure that exchanges parameters and the initial commitment to the key chain. Both are outside the scope of this memo. For SRTP, bootstrapping is assumed to happen out of band, possibly in the key management protocol that exchanges the SRTP parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: SRTP is a locked envelope for audio and video calls. TESLA is a new kind of lock for it, and the clock-setting and first handshake are left to someone else.

sections.title: The TESLA Extension and Packet Layout
sections.content:
TESLA is an OPTIONAL authentication transform. When used, each packet carries a TESLA authentication extension with three mandatory fields:

  • i: 32 bits, the identifier of the time interval whose key K_i was used for this packet's TESLA MAC.
  • Disclosed Key: variable length, the key K_(i-d), which lets receivers authenticate packets from earlier intervals.
  • TESLA MAC: variable length, computed with a key K'_i derived from K_i. That key is disclosed in a later packet.

The extension is inserted before the optional MKI and the recommended SRTP authentication tag. The two tags cannot sit side by side, because SRTP's MAC does not cover the MKI and SRTP could not be redefined to include it. So the MKI ends up between the TESLA MAC and the SRTP MAC.

The same extension is used in SRTCP, where the MKI is optional but the E-bit, the SRTCP index and the authentication tag are mandatory. This means the external SRTP MAC is mandatory with TESLA in SRTCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet gets a small label: which time slot it belongs to, a secret from an earlier slot that can now be shown, and a seal that can only be checked once its own secret is revealed later.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Processing
sections.content:
The sender follows RFC 3711 processing up to step 5, then picks the chain key for the current interval, builds the TESLA extension (the interval number, the key disclosed for the previous disclosure interval, and the TESLA MAC), appends the MKI if used, and computes the external SRTP tag if required. A key for interval i is disclosed in interval i+d.

The receiver first checks for replay. The replay list holds only packets already authenticated by TESLA, so replay list updates MUST NOT be based on the SRTP MAC. Next it checks the SRTP tag, which guards against denial of service. A packet that passes is buffered until a later packet discloses its key. If the interval number has jumped more than d intervals past the highest one seen, packets were lost and the missing keys MUST be computed from the newly disclosed key.

Once the key is known, the receiver runs TESLA verification, including the safety condition from RFC 4082. A failure means the packet MUST be discarded and the event SHOULD be logged. A packet judged unsafe is RECOMMENDED to be discarded and logged as well. Verifying before decryption is RECOMMENDED. The replay list is updated only after TESLA verification succeeds.
sections.plainLanguage: The listener keeps each message in a drawer without trusting it. When the speaker later shows the matching secret, the listener checks the seal and only then believes the message.

sections.title: TESLA MAC, PRFs and Default Parameters
sections.content:
For SRTP, the TESLA MAC covers the ROC (rollover counter) followed by the RTP header and encrypted payload. For SRTCP it covers the RTCP header (first 8 bytes) and the encrypted portion. The default and mandatory-to-support algorithm for both the pseudo-random function and the MAC is HMAC-SHA1, and the MAC output is truncated to its left-most n_m bits.

Two one-way functions are needed. F builds the key chain, defined as K_i = HMAC_SHA1(K_{i+1}, 0). F' derives the key actually used for the MAC, K'_i = HMAC_SHA1(K_i, 1).

The cryptographic context gains 11 parameters, including the PRF and MAC identifiers, the output lengths n_p, n_f and n_m, the session start T_0, the interval length T_int in msec, the disclosure delay d, the clock lag bound D_t, the chain length n_c and the committed initial key.

The defaults add 38 bytes to each packet, which for some applications is more than a 50% increase in packet size. Alternative settings are left to future RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: The secrets form a chain where each one can be made from the next but not the other way round. The speaker reveals them backwards, so a revealed secret can be checked but cannot be used to forge older messages.

sections.title: Bootstrapping, Clocks and Ending a Stream
sections.content:
TESLA MUST be bootstrapped at session setup, for the parameter exchange and the initial key commitment, through a regular data authentication system. A digital signature algorithm is RECOMMENDED. Sender and receiver also need to be loosely synchronized, with a known bound D_t on clock drift, and this memo assumes out-of-band schemes provide it.

Because each key rides in a later packet, TESLA tolerates loss: a key in a lost packet can be derived from a future one. The key stream does stop when the media stops, so null packets carrying TESLA keys SHOULD be sent for d intervals of duration t_int after the stream ends, at the average rate of the session media stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the show, the speaker proves who they are the old-fashioned way and everyone agrees on the time. After the last word, the speaker keeps sending empty messages so the final secrets still get out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since receivers must buffer packets before they can authenticate them, a flood of bogus packets can cause denial of service. The external SRTP MAC, based on the group key, MAY be added to stop outside attackers. It is RECOMMENDED to truncate it to 32 bits, since it only guards against external DoS. A forged packet would be accepted after about 2^31 attempts on average, and the forgery would then fail the TESLA check.

TESLA's security depends on the safety condition in RFC 4082, and on the bootstrapping, time synchronization and key management systems, which this memo does not cover. The default 80-bit TESLA MAC meets the requirement in RFC 2104 of at least 80 bits and at least half the hash output size.
sections.plainLanguage: A pile of unchecked messages could be stuffed with junk. A cheap quick check at the door keeps most junk out, and the real seal check catches the rest.
